title: Forms of Address Across the Spanish-Speaking World

sections.content: You know *tú* from A1 Unit 2, *usted* from A1 Unit 5, and *don*, *doña*, and Rioplatense *vos* from B2 Unit 34 (*hablás*, *comés*, *vivís*, *vos tenés*, *sos*, *vení*, *mirá*, *decime*). Across the Spanish-speaking world, singular address forms map differently onto intimacy, solidarity, and hierarchy depending on the region.

In systems dominated by *tuteo* (such as Mexico, Peru, the Caribbean, and Spain), *tú* is the default for symmetric closeness and youth solidarity, while *usted* marks formality, age deference, or institutional hierarchy. In the River Plate area (Argentina and Uruguay) and parts of Central America and Colombia, *voseo* replaces *tú* in everyday informal speech (*vos pensás*, *vos tenés*). Meanwhile, in parts of Colombia and Costa Rica, *ustedeo* extends *usted* into the home and close friendships as a warm marker of mutual respect rather than cold distance. At C1, you need to interpret these regional address shifts accurately and maintain consistent verb, clitic (*te* with *tú/vos* vs. *le/lo/la* and *se* with *usted*), and possessive (*tu* vs. *su*) agreement.

sections.title: Regional Singular Address Systems
rows: *Tuteo* (informal closeness in Mexico, Caribbean, Peru, Spain)
Tú tienes tu boleto y yo te llamo mañana.
*Voseo* (informal closeness in Argentina, Uruguay, Central America)
Vos tenés tu boleto y yo te llamo mañana. / Vení y decime qué pensás.
Usted tiene su boleto y yo le avisaré mañana, don Manuel.
Intimate *ustedeo* (family and close friends in parts of Colombia and Costa Rica)
Hermano, ¿usted ya habló con nuestra madre?

items.spanish: En Buenos Aires, el voseo pertenece al habla cotidiana de todas las generaciones: «Vos sabés que siempre podés contar conmigo».
items.english: In Buenos Aires, voseo belongs to the everyday speech of all generations: 'You know that you can always count on me'.

items.spanish: Aunque el verbo cambia en «vos tenés» o «vos sos», los pronombres átonos y el posesivo coinciden con el tuteo: «Te traje tu abrigo».
items.english: Although the verb changes in 'vos tenés' or 'vos sos', the unstressed pronouns and the possessive match tuteo: 'I brought you your coat'.

items.spanish: En algunas regiones colombianas, el ustedeo de cercanía convive con el cariño familiar: «Hijo, cuídese mucho y llámeme al llegar».
items.english: In some Colombian regions, intimate ustedeo coexists with family affection: 'Son, take good care of yourself and call me when you arrive'.

items.spanish: En un intercambio profesional, conviene mantener la concordancia de cortesía con «usted», «su» y «le» hasta que el interlocutor proponga el tuteo.
items.english: In a professional exchange, it is advisable to maintain polite agreement with 'usted', 'su', and 'le' until the interlocutor proposes using 'tú'.

sections.content: Notice how clitics pair with each pronoun: modern American *voseo* takes singular *te* and *tu* (*Vos te acordás de tu promesa*). Conversely, even when *usted* is used affectionately between close friends or siblings in *ustedeo*, its grammatical agreement remains third-person singular (*Hermano, ¿usted trajo su llave?*).
